summary: Reports actual measurements of mean round-trip times in the ARPANET.

eli5.summary: It records how long messages took to go to another computer and back, based on real measurements.

questions: how fast was the arpanet in 1974
subtitle: Measurements of message delays across the ARPANET from August and December 1973

tldr.problem: ARPANET operators need to understand how fast messages travel across the network, but no systematic measurements have been published.
tldr.mechanism: Naylor and Opderbeck at UCLA-NMC measure round-trip times during two seven-day periods in 1973, collecting data on every message and analyzing delays by source, destination, and hop count.
tldr.outcome: The measurements reveal that average round-trip time increased from 93 milliseconds in August to 132 milliseconds in December (excluding status reports), driven by changes in routing protocol overhead and network topology. The data shows RTT scales with distance, ranging from 27 milliseconds for local traffic to over 800 milliseconds for distant nodes.

today: RFC 619 is the first published systematic measurement of ARPANET latency. The methodology—measuring round-trip time, breaking it down by source, destination, and hop count, and correlating delays with network topology and traffic patterns—became the foundation for all subsequent network performance analysis and monitoring.

sections.title: Measuring Network Latency
sections.content: Naylor and Opderbeck at UCLA measured the time it took messages to travel through ARPANET and receive acknowledgment—the round-trip time (RTT). They collected data continuously for seven days in August 1973 and again in December 1973, capturing every message and its delay. They define RTT precisely: the time from when the source IMP (Interface Message Processor, or router) puts a message on the output queue until the source IMP receives the RFNM (Request For Next Message) acknowledgment from the destination IMP.
sections.eli5: They counted how long it took messages to get to their destination and back, over two weeks in 1973, so people could understand how fast the network was.

sections.title: Key Findings
sections.content: In August, with 2935 messages per minute, the average round-trip time was 93 milliseconds. In December, with fewer messages per minute (2226), the average RTT nearly doubled to 200 milliseconds. However, December's increase was partly due to status reports sent from each IMP to the Network Control Center (NCC); excluding those, the RTT was 132 milliseconds—still a significant increase. The measurements show that RTT scales sharply with distance: zero-hop traffic (local) averaged 27–41 milliseconds, while 10-hop traffic reached 939 milliseconds in December (or 410 milliseconds without status reports). The data includes detailed tables by source site and destination site, showing that some sites like ISI and SRI handled traffic efficiently while others, particularly those sending only status reports, experienced very high delays.
sections.eli5: Messages in December took longer to travel than in August. Local messages arrived in about 30 milliseconds, but messages traveling ten hops took nearly a second. Status reports got especially bogged down.

sections.title: Factors Affecting Performance
sections.content: Naylor and Opderbeck identify five key factors behind the RTT increase. First, routing messages—which every IMP sends to share topology information—more than doubled in frequency, from every 640 milliseconds in August to every 128 milliseconds in December, consuming more bandwidth and causing queuing delays. Second, the traffic matrix shifted: August's heavy traffic between nearby sites (like Ames and Amest) contributed to lower overall RTT. Third, network topology expanded, increasing the average number of hops from 3.24 to 4.02. Fourth, measurements capture bursts of traffic, not just averages. Fifth, host processing delays independent of network load can affect measured RTT. These factors show that RTT is not purely a function of distance but depends on routing overhead, traffic patterns, and network growth.
sections.eli5: The network got slower because routing messages took more bandwidth, traffic spread across more distant sites, and the network grew more hops. All of these slowed down message travel.

references.text: Kleinrock, L., Naylor, W., "On Measured Behavior of the ARPA Network", Network Measurement Group Note 18, NIC 20793.
